text:
anya: Heads-up — we need to settle on fallback behavior for staged canaries under bursty traffic. Right now the router queues requests until a slow canary drains and that can cause head-of-line blocking for other customers.

miguel: Agree. We saw this in the last release spike. What are the constraints? latency SLOs, per-tenant fairness, and cost (can't just route everyone to big models).

sam: +1. We should think about a two-tier fallback: fast degraded path (smaller/quantized model) and slow queued path. Router needs to decide per-request.

tiffany: For the router contract: it should have clear signals from runtime: capacity_available, est_latency_ms, and queue_depth. Then router picks route based on policy.

liam: Prefer policy based on SLO budget + estimated cost. If tenant is within latency budget, send to canary. If not, either route to fallback variant or reject with a 429.

anya: Thinking about burst protection: staggered admission windows per-tenant. Each tenant gets a token bucket for canary admission. During bursts, some tokens are consumed and subsequent requests go to fallback. Keeps canary stable.

miguel: Token bucket per-tenant + global soft-cap per-canary instance seems reasonable. But how do we recover tokens after a canary warms back up? Need a probe to keep tokens healthy.

sam: We could emit a periodic probe request (cheap synthetic) every N seconds to measure tail latency. If probe latency < threshold, replenish tokens faster. If probe fails, start draining.

tiffany: Probe signal should feed into telemetry and also to the router as a boolean "canary_healthy" for quick checks. Avoid too-frequent probes to not bias metrics.

liam: Also: allow a circuit override for critical tenants (enterprise commits) to bypass token limits. But that requires an explicit per-tenant opt-in and accounting.

anya: Implementation sketch (router pseudocode):

```
if tenant.has_override: route(canary)
elif canary.token_bucket.try_consume(1): route(canary)
elif fallback.variant_available: route(fallback)
else: return 429
```

sam: Nice. For fallback variants, we need compatibility rules: same API, same structured outputs or a declared translator. Fallback can also be a cached response if identical prompt seen recently.

migueI: typo ^^ (miguel) — also consider an intermediate queue that accepts low-priority requests for best-effort fulfillment when canary recovers, but keep a max wait time to avoid unbounded latency.

anya: Good call. Keep max_wait configurable per-tenant. If queued beyond max_wait, escalate to fallback or cancel.

devops-bot: deploybot: canary-fallback/v2 config pushed to staging at 1715004400 :white_check_mark:

tiffany: Ops question — where do we store token bucket state? Redis (fast) vs local router memory (less cross-router fairness). Leaning Redis for global fairness.

sam: Use Redis with tenant sharding and fallback local cache. On Redis outage, routers should degrade to local best-effort token buckets and mark global_mode=false.

liam: Telemetry: emit per-request decision tag: route_choice={canary|fallback|queue|reject}, token_bucket_remaining, canary_probe_latency_ms. That should help tune thresholds.

anya: Follow-ups: 1) Draft router <-> runtime signal contract (capacity_available, est_latency_ms, healthy_probe) 2) Prototype token-bucket + probe in staging and run synthetic burst tests 3) Add per-tenant override and queue with max_wait.

miguel: I'll pick up the signal contract doc.

sam: I'll prototype token-bucket + queue shim.

tiffany: I'll add telemetry fields to the spec.

liam: Happy to help with SLA/cost tradeoff matrix.

anya: Thanks — let's sync in tomorrow's infra sync (11:00). :spiral_calendar:
